explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but Paul actually goes the other way. Paul, the apostle writing this letter to Timothy, opens with "This is a trustworthy saying: If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task." That's no warning label. He calls the task noble.

That's right. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says whoever aspires to be an overseer "…desires a noble task." He doesn't say it's reaching too much. The list of requirements comes after that, but the first word on the job is noble.

That's right, it's in the list: an overseer must be "…able to teach…" It sits in verse 2 right next to respectable and hospitable. So the overseer is a teacher as well as a host. I've pressed a lot of dough, and I'll tell you, explaining WHY you press it is half the job.

Look again at verse 2, because it's right there in the list. An overseer must be "…above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach…" Teaching is part of the job description. This one's easy to skim past when the list is moving fast.

Yes! Paul says an overseer must be "…not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money." Notice it's the LOVE of money, not money itself. Gentle, peaceable and free of that love all sit together in one verse (1 Timothy 3:3).

Fear of man feels like it belongs on a list like this, and I'd have guessed it too. I get jumpy every time a fresh batch comes out of the oven. But it isn't on Paul's list here. In verse 3 he says an overseer must be "…free of the love of money."
That one isn't in Paul's list here. If worry kept you off the list, I'd be disqualified before my first batch cooled. What Paul says is that an overseer must be free of the love of money.

explanations.answer: It shows if he can care for God's church
explanations.explanation: You got it. Paul asks it straight out: "For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God?" His own home is where it shows. A man who can't run a kitchen has no business running the bakery, and I say that as someone who once lost a fight with a cooling rack.

explanations.answer: His family will help him lead the church
explanations.explanation: That's a nice thought, but Paul never says it. What he asks is a question: if someone does not know how to manage his own household, "…how can he care for the church of God?" Family helping to lead isn't in the verse.

explanations.answer: The church will gather in his house
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention a meeting place in this verse. What he asks is a question: if someone does not know how to manage his own household, "…how can he care for the church of God?" That question is the reason he gives in verse 5.

That's the word. Paul says a recent convert "…may become conceited and fall under the same condemnation as the devil." A new believer put in charge could get a swelled head. I've seen a cookie get puffed up in the oven, and that doesn't end well either.
Makes sense, but that's not Paul's word. He says a recent convert "…may become conceited and fall under the same condemnation as the devil." The danger he names is a big head, not a low heart.

Careless sounds right, like forgetting the oven mitt, but it isn't what Paul writes. He says the recent convert "…may become conceited and fall under the same condemnation as the devil." (1 Timothy 3:6). The word he uses is conceited.

explanations.answer: So he won't fall into disgrace and the devil's snare
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Paul says he must have a good reputation with outsiders "…so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the snare of the devil." The neighbors' opinion matters. It's a protection for the overseer himself.

explanations.answer: So more outsiders will want to join the church
explanations.explanation: That sounds reasonable, but Paul doesn't say it. He gives his reason in the verse: "…so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the snare of the devil." Outsiders joining isn't what he mentions. Stick with what he says.

explanations.answer: So the city's rulers will protect the church
explanations.explanation: Paul never says anything about rulers in this passage. The reason he gives is "…so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the snare of the devil." A good name with outsiders keeps the overseer from that fall. That's the only reason on the page.
That's it. Paul says, "…they must first be tested. Then, if they are above reproach, let them serve as deacons." Test first, serve second. Nobody just gets handed the apron and a title.
I can see why you'd pick it, but elected isn't Paul's word. He says deacons "…must first be tested." Then, if they are above reproach, they serve. So the test comes before serving as a deacon.

Training sounds right, friend, but Paul's word is different. He says deacons "…must first be tested." Only after that, if they are above reproach, do they serve as deacons (1 Timothy 3:10). The key word is tested.

Yes! Paul says the women must be "…dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things." He tucks it right into his lines about deacons. Slander is words used to tear somebody down, and he's clear it has no place here.

Lazy isn't in this verse, friend. Paul says the women must be "…dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things." The word he uses is slanderers. If lazy were on the list, my snooze button and I would be in big trouble.

Fearful feels like it should fit, and I'd have said it too. I once jumped when my own apron string tapped me. But Paul says the women must be "…dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things." The word in the verse is slanderers.
That's right. Paul says, "A deacon must be the husband of but one wife…" It's the same line he gave for the overseer back in verse 2. He doesn't change it for deacons.

Paul says it plainly in verse 12: "A deacon must be the husband of but one wife…" That's the same line he used for the overseer. So the deacon gets the same requirement. Easy to miss when the list is moving.

explanations.answer: High standing and great confidence in the faith
explanations.explanation: You got it. Paul says those who have served well as deacons "…acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus." That's what they walk away with. It's better than a gold star on the fridge.

explanations.answer: A larger share of the church's offerings
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a thing about offerings. What he says is that those who serve well "…acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus." The reward he names is standing and confidence. Nothing about getting a bigger cut.

explanations.answer: A seat among the overseers of the church
explanations.explanation: That would be a promotion, but Paul doesn't promise it here. He says those who serve well as deacons gain "…a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus." That's the reward he gives in verse 13.

That's the word. Paul writes so Timothy will know "…how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God…" The church is a household, a family under one roof. That's a warm picture for a church to hold.
Kingdom is a real Bible word, but it's not the one Paul uses here. He says Timothy needs to know how each one must conduct himself in "God's household." The church is described as a household.

City is a nice guess, friend, but it's not in the verse. Paul says each one must conduct himself in "…God’s household, which is the church of the living God…" So the church is called a household here.

Yes, that's word for word what Paul says. God's household "…is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth." Pillar and foundation: that's what holds the whole building up. A pretty big job for a bunch of folks sitting in rows.

It's true, and Paul says it right there in verse 15. God's household is "…the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth." Nothing sneaky in that one. Sometimes a statement is just straight Scripture.
Yes! Paul writes, "By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great…" Common confession means it's said by believers together. He isn't pointing to a few specialists.
Paul doesn't narrow it to the apostles. He says, "By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great…" Common means shared, said together, not locked in a small group.
That makes it sound like a secret club, friend, and Paul says the opposite. It's "By common confession…" which means it's held in common. Not by a few. It's a shared confession of the faith.

The confession says more than that. The line is "…was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world…" That reaches far past Israel. Nations and the whole world are way bigger than one people.
Right, it's false. The confession says He "…was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world…" That reaches far past Israel. Paul's line names the nations and the world.
